title: 📘 UNIT 7: STATES, PRINCIPALITIES, POPULATION MOVEMENTS & INTERACTIONS IN ETHIOPIA, 13th–MID-16th C.
📌 7.1 THE “SOLOMONIC” DYNASTY & THE CHRISTIAN KINGDOM
notes:
👑 Yekuno-Amlak

Yekuno-Amlak was a local ruler from Amhara who came to power in 1270 and established the dynasty known as the “Solomonic” dynasty.

He claimed descent from the Aksumite kings and used the tradition of Queen of Sheba and King Solomon to justify his legitimacy.

title: 📜 The “Solomonic” Claim
notes:
The claim that the rulers descended from King Solomon is presented as a legend rather than a historically proven fact.

📖 The Kibre Negest, written in the 14th century, developed the tradition that the Ethiopian ruling class descended from Menilek I, son of the Queen of Sheba and King Solomon.

Ethiopian monarchs from Yekuno-Amlak to Emperor Haile Silassie I claimed descent from Menilek I.

title: 🗺️ Christian Kingdom in 1270
notes:
When Yekuno-Amlak came to power, the Christian Kingdom was confined mainly to:

• Southern Eritrea
• Tigray
• Lasta
• Northern Shewa

The rulers later expanded the territory of the Christian Kingdom.

title: ⚔️ Expansion of the Christian Kingdom
notes:
👑 Amde Seyon was one of the major expansionist rulers of the Christian Kingdom.

The kingdom expanded its political influence over several regions and states.

📌 Expansion was connected with:
• Territorial control
• Tribute collection
• Control of trade routes
• Expansion of Christianity
• Strengthening royal authority

title: 🏛️ Rist, Gult and Bale-Gult Systems
notes:
🌾 Rist Right
A hereditary claim to land. It was a communal birthright to land, and peasants paid tribute to the state.

🏛️ Gult Right
Land or revenue rights given to state officials in return for service. It functioned as a medieval substitute for salary and was not hereditary.

👤 Bale-Gult
A person given authority over an area was responsible for maintaining law and order. The system helped administer the large Christian empire and maintain a large territorial army.

title: ⛪ Church and State
notes:
The rulers of the “Solomonic” dynasty maintained political and cultural traditions associated with Aksum and Zagwe.

✝️ Christianity continued to expand.

👑 Political and religious authority were closely connected.

🌍 Foreign relations continued with Egypt and the Middle East and expanded toward Europe, especially Portugal and Spain.

title: 📌 7.2 THE MUSLIM PRINCIPALITIES
notes:
☪️ The spread of Islam and long-distance trade contributed to the establishment of several Muslim Sultanates in Ethiopia and the Horn.

The Zeila trade route was an important gateway through which Islam reached the interior of Ethiopia.

Major Muslim principalities included:
• Ifat
• Fatigar
• Dawaro
• Dara
• Bali
• Hadya
• Arbabini
• Sharka
• Adal

title: 🏙️ Sultanate of Ifat
notes:
📍 Ifat emerged south of Shewa.

👑 Founder: Umar Walasma
📅 1285: The Walasma dynasty replaced the older Makhzumite dynasty.

Ifat became the strongest Muslim Sultanate in the region and controlled important sections of the Zeila trade route.

⚔️ It became the strongest rival of the Christian highland state.

title: 🛤️ Trade and Muslim Principalities
notes:
Trade was an important factor in the rise and development of Muslim Sultanates.

💰 Trade provided livelihood and wealth.

🛤️ Trade routes connected different peoples and states.

⚔️ Control of profitable trade routes also became a major source of conflict between the Christian Kingdom and Muslim Sultanates.

title: 🕌 Other Muslim Sultanates
notes:
📍 Fatigar: Emerged around the middle of the 13th century south of present-day Bulga around Shenkora.

📍 Dawaro: Located between the middle Awash River and upper Wabe-Shebele.

📍 Bali: Located south of the Wabe-Shebele in a rich area.

📍 Dara: Located between Dawaro and Bali.

📍 Arbabini: Located between Dawaro and Hadiya.

📍 Hadiya: Located west of Dawaro and Bali.

📍 Sharka: Located in present-day Arsi.

title: 🏴 Sultanate of Adal
notes:
The Walasma family established the Sultanate of Adal around Harar in 1367 after Ifat became vulnerable to Christian expansion.

📍 First centre: Dakar, southeast of Harar
📍 1520: Centre moved to Harar
📍 1576/77: Capital later moved to Awsa because of the defeat of Imam Ahmed and Oromo expansion.

Adal became an important centre of resistance against the Christian Kingdom.

title: 📌 7.3 CHRISTIAN KINGDOM & SULTANATE OF ADAL, 1520s–1559
notes:
⚔️ The major source of conflict was competition for control of long-distance trade routes.

Other causes included:
• Desire for territorial expansion
• Competition for economic wealth
• Control of the Zeila trade route

🔥 The major war reached its height between 1529 and 1543.

title: 🕌 Imam Ahmed ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi
notes:
Imam Ahmed ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi became the major leader of Adal during the conflict.

He mobilized Afar, Argoba, Somali, Harari and other communities and organized them against the Christian Kingdom.

⚔️ His military campaigns against Lebne-Dengel began in 1527.

title: ⚔️ Shimbra Kure, 1529
notes:
📅 March 1529
📍 Shimbra Kure, near present-day Mojjo

Imam Ahmed's forces defeated the Christian army.

After this victory, Adal forces continued their campaigns and gained control over territories including:

• Bali
• Dawaro
• Fatagar
• Sidama
• Hadiya
• Kambata

title: 🌍 International Intervention
notes:
The conflict became international when Portugal and Ottoman Turkey intervened.

🇹🇷 Ottoman Turkey supported Imam Ahmed with military assistance, including musketeers.

🇵🇹 Portugal sent soldiers to support the Christian Kingdom after an earlier request from Lebne-Dengel.

title: ⚔️ Woyna-Dega, 1543
notes:
📅 February 25, 1543
📍 Near Lake Tana

The combined forces of Emperor Gelawdewos and the Portuguese defeated Imam Ahmed's forces.

Imam Ahmed was killed during the battle.

🏆 The Christian Kingdom regained control over much of the northern and central plateau.

title: ⚔️ Adal and the Christian Kingdom After 1543
notes:
After Imam Ahmed's death, Adal was reorganized under Emir Nur ibn al-Waazir Mujahid.

📅 1559: Nur's forces fought Emperor Gelawdewos and killed him.

The prolonged wars weakened both the Christian Kingdom and Adal through enormous losses of human and material resources.

title: 🤝 Christian–Muslim Interactions
notes:
Despite warfare, Christian and Muslim societies interacted economically, socially and culturally.

🛒 Trade remained a major channel of integration.

Merchants travelled between the highlands and the coast.

These interactions encouraged:
• Trade
• Intermarriage
• Linguistic interaction
• Religious interaction
• Cultural exchange

title: 📌 7.4 SOUTHERN & CENTRAL STATES OF ETHIOPIA
notes:
Several peoples and states existed in central and southern Ethiopia during this period.

Major examples included:
• Damot
• Kafa
• Ennarya
• Bizamo
• Wolaita
• Yem
• Kambata
• Gurage chiefdoms
• Agaw Kingdom of Gojjam

title: 🏛️ Damot
notes:
Damot was probably the earliest of the listed states and may have existed as early as the Aksumite period.

📍 Territory: Areas south of the Blue Nile River

👑 Important ruler: Motalami

✝️ Motalami was converted to Christianity by Abune Tekle Haymanot in the late 13th century.

📅 1316: King Amde Seyon annexed Damot into the Christian state.

title: 🌿 Ennarya, Kafa & Wolaita
notes:
🌿 Ennarya
Probably existed north of the Gojeb River and later became part of the Christian highland Kingdom.

🌿 Kafa
Known at least since the end of the 14th century and remained an independent kingdom from the Christian highland state.

🌿 Wolaita
Had strong connections with Damot. Its ruling dynasty was known as Wolaita-Malla. It paid tribute to King Yeshaq and may have remained connected with the Christian empire until the wars of Ahmad ibn Ibrahim.

title: 🏔️ Kambata, Gurage & Gojjam
notes:
🏔️ Kambata: One of the states in the central Ethiopian highlands.

🏘️ Gurage Chiefdoms: Concentrated west of Lake Zeway and in the highlands of Dawaro. Chiefs used titles such as Azmach, Abegaz and Nigus.

🌊 Agaw Kingdom of Gojjam: Located south of Lake Tana and exercised strong control over the lake and its islands.

📅 Early 14th century: Amde Tseyon incorporated Gojjam into the Christian state.

title: 💰 Economy of Southern & Central States
notes:
The economy of many southern and central states was based mainly on agriculture and trade.

Important trade items included:
• Enslaved people
• Civet
• Ivory
• Other natural products

Enslaved people were in high demand in Arabia, Persia and India.

title: 📌 7.5 POPULATION MOVEMENTS, EXPANSION & INTEGRATION
notes:
🌍 The 16th century was characterized by wars and major population movements in the Horn of Africa.

Major population movements discussed include:
• Argoba
• Afar
• Somali
• Oromo

📌 The largest population movement and expansion during this period was that of the Oromo.

title: 👥 Argoba Movement
notes:
The Argoba lived along important caravan routes leading to Zeila.

🛤️ They played important roles in trade and the formation of Muslim Sultanates such as Shewa and Ifat.

⚔️ Their homeland became an area of conflict between the Christian Kingdom and Muslim Sultanates.

The wars contributed to the dispersal of Argoba settlement.

title: 🐪 Afar Movement
notes:
Drought contributed to the movement of the Afar toward the east until they reached the middle Awash.

🛤️ Important trade routes passed through Afar territory.

⚔️ Competition between the Christian Kingdom and Muslim Sultanates over trade routes placed pressure on the Afar to move in different directions.

Their pastoral economy helped them survive the destructive effects of warfare.

title: 🐪 Somali Movement
notes:
The Somali inhabited areas crossed by important medieval trade routes.

Before the wars of Imam Ahmed, demographic pressure contributed to Somali population movement.

The movement strengthened Imam Ahmed's military power.

📅 After Imam Ahmed's defeat in 1543, much of the Somali population returned toward its home areas.

title: 🌿 Oromo Homeland & Movement
notes:
The Oromo are an indigenous Cushitic people of Ethiopia and the Horn of Africa.

📍 Traditional homeland before the 16th century: southeastern Ethiopian highlands.

🏛️ Political and religious centre: Madda Walabu, around the Bale-Sidama borderlands.

Major causes of movement:
• Demographic pressure
• Need for additional land
• Growth of human and livestock populations
• Conflicts between Christian Kingdoms and Muslim Sultanates

title: 🧭 Oromo Confederacies & Directions
notes:
Two major Oromo confederacies existed before the large population movement:

🟢 Borana Confederacy
Mecha, Tulama, southern Borana and Guji clans.

🟠 Barentu Confederacy
Karayu, Marawa, Ittu, Humbana, Akachu, Wollo and Arsi clans.

📅 Major movement and expansion: 1522–1618

Barentu generally moved northeast, while Borana moved north-west. Oromo groups also moved toward Kenya and Somalia.

title: 📊 Two Phases of Oromo Movement
notes:
1️⃣ First Phase
Early 16th century: relatively gradual movement.

2️⃣ Second Phase
Middle of the 16th century to 1618: large-scale movement involving the use of force.

The Oromo moved north through the area between Mount Walabu and Lake Abaya, then toward the Rift Valley and other regions.

title: ⚔️ Oromo Butta Wars, 1522–1618
notes:
The Oromo fought twelve Butta wars during their expansion.

Important Gadaa periods included:

• Melba, 1522–1530: defeated Batra Amora and occupied Bali.
• Mudena, 1530–1538: reached the Awash River.
• Kilole, 1538–1546: controlled Dawaro.
• Bifole, 1546–1554: advanced to Waj and Erer.
• Michille, 1554–1562: achieved victories against several forces.
• Harmufa, 1562–1570: occupied areas including Angot, Ganzyi and Sayint.

title: ⚔️ Later Oromo Expansion
notes:
• Robale, 1570–1578: fought the forces of Sartsa Dingil.
• Birmaji, 1578–1586: controlled Ar'ine in Waj and crossed the Jama area.
• Mul'ata, 1586–1594: seized Damot, Bizamo, Gafat, Dambiya and Tigray.
• Dulo, 1594–1602
• Melba, 1603–1610
• Mudena, 1610–1618: expanded toward western and northern parts of the Horn.

title: 🏛️ Oromo Gadaa Centres
notes:
Different Oromo branches established Gadaa centres during their movement.

📍 Oda Nabee: Tulama, East Shewa

📍 Oda Roba: Sikko-Mando, Arsi

📍 Oda Bultum: Itu-Humbenna, Hararge

📍 Oda Bisil: Mecha, West Shewa

📍 Oda Bulluq: Jawwi Mecha, Horro-Guduru

title: 🌍 Consequences of Oromo Expansion
notes:
The Oromo population movement brought major changes to the Ethiopian region.

• Ethnic and cultural intermixing increased.
• Old states such as Damot, Bizamo and Ennarya were destroyed or transformed.
• Some populations were assimilated or displaced.
• The Christian Kingdom was weakened territorially and financially.
• The political centre of the Christian Kingdom shifted northward toward Lake Tana and Gondar.
• Adal was reduced largely to Harar.
• Oromo communities increasingly became sedentary agriculturists.
• Many Oromo later adopted Christianity and Islam.

title: 📌 7.6 GADAA SYSTEM OF THE OROMO
notes:
🏛️ Gadaa is an age-grade based system of social, political, economic and religious organization.

It helped the Oromo:
• Organize society
• Administer affairs
• Defend territories
• Maintain law and order
• Manage economic activities
• Resolve conflicts
• Protect women's rights
• Build social cohesion

title: 🗳️ Democratic Features of Gadaa
notes:
The Gadaa system contained important democratic principles:

• Periodic succession of political power
• Power-sharing
• Representation of lineages, clans and confederacies
• Division of responsibilities
• Accountability
• Rule of law
• Check and balance
• Balanced opposition

📅 One Gadaa period lasted eight years.

title: 👥 Gadaa Age Grades
notes:
The Oromo system organized people into age grades and generation sets.

📌 Common age-grade structure:

• Dabale: Birth–8 years, socialization
• Game: 9–16 years, socialization
• Folle: 17–24 years, military training and agriculture
• Qondala: 25–32 years, military service
• Raba-Dori: 33–40 years, candidates for political power
• Gadaa: 41–48 years, leaders of Gadaa government
• Yuba: 49–80 years, senior advisors, educators and ritual leaders

title: 👑 Abba Gadaa & Gadaa Leadership
notes:
👑 Abba Gadaa: Head of the Gadaa government and spokesman of the ruling generation set.

Other important officials included:
• Abba Bokku: Father of the scepter
• Abba Chaffe: Head of the assembly
• Abba-Dula: War leader
• Abba Sera: Father of law
• Abba Alanga: Judge
• Abba Sa'a: Father of treasury

⚖️ Abba Gadaa did not possess absolute power. Supreme authority rested with the Chaffe assembly.

title: 🌳 Chaffe, Odaa & Gumi-Gayo
notes:
🌳 Chaffe was the assembly of the ruling Gadaa class.

The assembly traditionally met under an Odaa tree, symbolizing dialogue and consensus.

🏛️ Gumi-Gayo was an assembly of representatives of the wider society and mainly served as a law-making body.

Representatives discussed laws to be introduced, repealed or amended.

title: ⚖️ Principles of Gadaa Governance
notes:
Gadaa governance emphasized:

• Eight-year succession
• Division of power
• Balanced opposition
• Power-sharing
• Rule of law
• Accountability
• Confession and impeachment, called buqqisu
• Testing period between election and investiture
• Checks and balances

title: 👩 Women and Sinqe
notes:
Women maintained rights through the Sinqe institution, which promoted sisterhood and solidarity.

Women participated in:
• Power transfer
• Conflict resolution
• Thanksgiving
• Social and cultural activities

The kalale were also privileged to support and advise the ruling class.

title: 📌 7.7 MOGGASA AND GUDDIFACHA
notes:
🤝 The Oromo used two major adoption mechanisms to incorporate non-Oromo people.

👶 Guddifacha
A system in which a parent adopted a child. The adopted child enjoyed equal rights and privileges with a biological child.

🤝 Moggasa
A system of incorporating non-Oromo individuals or groups into a clan through an oath of allegiance.

title: 🤝 Features of Moggasa
notes:
Through Moggasa, an incorporated person or community:

• Became a member of the clan.
• Received rights and obligations of membership.
• Received protection.
• Shared material benefits.
• Participated in the social life of the Oromo.

The Abba Gadaa undertook Moggasa on behalf of the clan.

title: 🌍 Effects of Moggasa & Guddifacha
notes:
These adoption systems helped different peoples live together and contributed to:

• Social cohesion
• Integration
• Cultural exchange
• Exchange of institutions
• Revival of long-distance trade
• Incorporation of neighbouring populations

Some neighbouring peoples adopted aspects of the Gadaa system and Oromo language, while Oromo communities also adopted cultures and traditions from peoples they encountered.

title: 📌 7.8 EGALITARIAN SYSTEM OF GOVERNANCE
notes:
⚖️ The textbook discusses egalitarian systems of governance among:

• Sidama
• Gedeo
• Konso
• Burji

An egalitarian system emphasizes participation, consultation, shared responsibilities and social equality.

title: 🌿 Sidama Governance
notes:
👑 Mote: King who exercised political and administrative authority.

👥 Songo: Council of elders that discussed issues and submitted decisions to the Mote.

🌿 Woma: Cultural and ritual leader and a person of peace.

The Sidama did not have a written constitution; rules were preserved through generations and practiced traditionally.

title: 🌿 Sidama Luwa System
notes:
The Luwa system organized Sidama society through age cycles.

📅 One age-grade cycle lasted eight years.

Five Luwa generations included:
• Fulasa
• Wawasa
• Darara
• Hirbora
• Mogisa

Each age group selected a leader called Gadaanna to represent its generation.

title: ⚖️ Egalitarian Governance: Key Features
notes:
Common characteristics emphasized in the traditional systems include:

• Consultation
• Council-based decision-making
• Participation of community members
• Respect for elders
• Traditional laws and customs
• Conflict resolution
• Shared responsibilities
• Protection of community interests

title: 🧠 UNIT 7 QUICK REVISION
notes:
👑 1270: Yekuno-Amlak established the so-called “Solomonic” dynasty.

🏛️ Rist: Hereditary communal land right.

🏛️ Gult: State service-based right, not hereditary.

☪️ Ifat: Major Muslim Sultanate founded by Umar Walasma.

🏴 Adal: Strong Muslim centre of resistance around Harar.

⚔️ 1529: Imam Ahmed defeated the Christian army at Shimbra Kure.

⚔️ 1543: Imam Ahmed was killed at Woyna-Dega; Adal forces were defeated by the combined Christian and Portuguese forces.

⚔️ 1559: Emir Nur Mujahid killed Emperor Gelawdewos.

🌍 16th century: Major population movements, especially Oromo expansion.

🏛️ Gadaa: Oromo age-grade system with eight-year political succession.

🤝 Guddifacha: Adoption of a child with equal rights to a biological child.

🤝 Moggasa: Incorporation of non-Oromo individuals or groups into a clan through allegiance.

⚖️ Egalitarian governance: Traditional participatory systems including those of Sidama, Gedeo, Konso and Burji.
